title: What you are about to see
blurb: This project is building a language model that thinks in careful steps. This opening section covers what it is, the colours and tags, and the words you need. Parts 1 to 8 and a wrap-up follow.

scenes.heading: A research project, not a product

caption.text: This is a research project. It is building a language model: a program that reads text and writes an answer.
Two of its goals: skills and careful thinking first, then learning from only a few examples.
It is not an app. GitHub lists 0 releases for it, and nothing here is finished.

Second goal: learning from only a few examples. Only partly shown so far: brand-new kinds of rule are mostly missed.

scenes.heading: The whole machine in one picture

caption.text: The reader gives each letter a meaning from the whole question. Its main part is borrowed from others and frozen: our practice never changes it.
The thinker thinks in rounds, which are laps of looking and thinking. Our practice sets its settings from scratch.
The calculator is ordinary code, not AI. It takes a text request and replies with text.
The stop switch says done. It is built, but never run.
The talker writes the final answer. Today it is a small stand-in.

scenes.heading: One picture for the whole video

caption.text: One picture runs through the whole video: a student doing a word problem.
A translator reads the question. A team of note-takers thinks it over, round after round.
The call writer, our team leader, writes a request slip. A pocket calculator hands back a slip with the result.
A little bell rings when they are done. One person writes the final answer. Each colour always means the same part.

scenes.heading: How sure are we? Three tags

Grey: placeholder. It does not exist yet. Example: the English talker.

scenes.heading: Two words: vector and round

caption.text: A vector is a list of numbers, like a note card. The reader turns each letter into one. “Picture only” means a drawing, not a measurement.
A round is one lap of looking at the whole question, passing notes, and thinking. The thinker does several laps.

scenes.heading: Two more words: call and reply

caption.text: A call is a text request to the calculator. Here, sub 12 5 means: take 5 away from 12.
The reply is the calculator's answer, also text: 7. Together they read sub 12 5 = 7.
The model writes calls itself. It may also write nothing, when no exact arithmetic is needed.

scenes.heading: Two more words: practice and kept aside

caption.text: Practice: the model tries a question, is told the right answer, and every setting is nudged a tiny bit. One nudge is one update.
Questions kept aside are never used in practice. They are saved for the exam, so the score is fair: the model has never seen them.

scenes.heading: Score and copy

caption.text: A score is points out of 100: the share of questions answered right. Here, 73.01 points on 6,040 questions kept aside.
A copy is one separate run of the model from its own random start. Six copies are six chances to see the same result.
Careful: 73.01 is one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design.

scenes.heading: The plain model: our yardstick

caption.text: A plain model is an ordinary model of the same size, trained on the same practice, with the same borrowed reader. It is our yardstick.
On the same 6,040 questions kept aside, the plain model scored 67.12 points out of 100, and ours scored 73.01.
Careful: these two scores come from one copy, at the smallest size, on an earlier design. We do not claim it holds at bigger sizes.
